site.name: meadowos
site.summary: meadowos-clone Fictional self-hosted home OS "MeadowOS" marketing site (magazine / zine-style long-scroll narrative). Pages | File | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `index.html` | Single-page long scroll: thin top nav + progress bar; hero with hand-drawn SVG house and flower illustration; five chapters (Roman numerals I–V) of magazine-prose with pull quotes and chapter illustrations; mid-page "Garden" 6-card plant-app grid (Nextfile / Bramble / Cottage / Smithy / Hearth / Postcard); reviewer quotes; terminal-style .iso download block + platform pills + minimum / recommended specs; six numbered manifesto items; dark footer | | `styles.css` | Brand color #2F5233 dark green, accent terracotta + wheat yellow, cream paper background; Crimson Pro serif + Inter; cards with slight rotate + paper-shadow; responsive | | `script.js` | Top scroll progress bar; smooth anchor scrolling; clicking "Download .iso" triggers a fake download-progress modal (increments to 100% then shows SHA256 verification passed) |

run_plan.goal: Exhaustively explore and critique the UX of the MeadowOS single-page marketing site, validating the long-scroll narrative, interactive elements, download flow, and responsive mobile layout.
run_plan.summary: The exploration will proceed through the single-page long-scroll site in a top-to-bottom sequence, validating navigation, narrative sections, and the Garden app grid. It will then trigger and validate the fake download modal and its completion state. Finally, the entire flow will be repeated on a mobile viewport to assess responsive behavior and tap target sizing.
assumptions: The site is entirely contained within index.html with no external routing or separate documentation pages.
The 'Docs' and 'Get the .iso' links perform smooth scrolling to anchored sections rather than navigating away.
The 'GitHub' and 'Matrix room' links are placeholder links (href='#') and will not navigate to external domains.
The download modal triggered by the .iso button is the only significant dynamic state on the page.
risk_hotspots: Small tap targets in the top navigation (Story, Garden, Docs) and footer (GitHub, Matrix) which failed the 44px mobile guidance.
The fake download modal flow: ensuring it increments correctly, displays the SHA256 verification state, and can be dismissed without trapping the user.
Long-scroll readability and visual hierarchy on mobile viewports, particularly for the five chapters of magazine-prose.
The 6-card Garden grid (Nextfile, Bramble, etc.) maintaining proper layout and slight rotate/paper-shadow styling on smaller screens.

phases.title: Hero and Navigation Validation
phases.objective: Validate the initial viewport, top navigation functionality, and scroll progress bar.
key_checks: Verify the hero section renders correctly with the hand-drawn SVG house and flower illustration.
Click the 'Story', 'Garden', and 'Docs' nav links to confirm smooth anchor scrolling to their respective sections.
Scroll down the page and verify the top scroll progress bar updates accurately.
Check the 'Read time · ~6 min' indicator is visible and properly styled.
exit_criteria: All top nav links successfully scroll to their anchored sections.
Progress bar responds to scroll position.
Hero section and SVG are fully visible without layout shifts.

phases.title: Narrative and Garden Grid
phases.objective: Validate the long-scroll narrative chapters (I-V) and the mid-page Garden app grid interactions.
key_checks: Scroll through all five chapters (Roman numerals I–V) verifying typography, pull quotes, and chapter illustrations.
Inspect the 'Garden' 6-card grid (Nextfile, Bramble, Cottage, Smithy, Hearth, Postcard) for correct layout and paper-shadow/rotate styling.
Hover over or interact with the Garden cards to check for any hover states or additional information.
Verify reviewer quotes section renders correctly between chapters and grid.
exit_criteria: All five chapters have been scrolled through and visible text/illustrations verified.
Garden grid displays all 6 cards with intended styling.
No text overflow or layout breakage observed in the prose sections.

phases.title: Download Flow and Manifesto
phases.objective: Validate the terminal-style download block, the fake download modal interaction, and the manifesto section.
key_checks: Scroll to the download section and verify the terminal-style block, platform pills, and minimum/recommended specs are displayed.
Click the 'Download · meadowos-0.7.iso · 1.2 GB' button.
Verify the fake download-progress modal appears and increments to 100%.
Verify the modal displays the 'SHA256 verification passed' message upon completion.
Dismiss the modal and ensure it closes properly.
Scroll to the six numbered manifesto items and verify they render correctly.
exit_criteria: Download modal successfully triggers, progresses, and shows SHA256 success state.
Modal can be dismissed without errors.
Terminal block, specs, and manifesto items are fully visible.

phases.title: Footer and Mobile Responsiveness
phases.objective: Validate the dark footer and then repeat critical checks on a mobile viewport to assess responsiveness and tap targets.
key_checks: Scroll to the dark footer and verify content and layout.
Switch viewport to mobile mode.
Re-evaluate the top navigation tap targets (Story, Garden, Docs) for the previously flagged small tap target warnings.
Verify the Garden 6-card grid stacks or adapts appropriately on mobile.
Trigger the download flow again on mobile to ensure the modal is responsive and usable.
Check footer links (GitHub, Matrix room) for tap target sizing on mobile.
exit_criteria: Mobile viewport displays all sections without horizontal overflow.
Tap target constraints and responsive layout adaptations have been assessed.

coverage_targets.pages: 100% coverage of the single index.html page, including all anchored sections.
coverage_targets.features: 100% coverage of interactive elements: all nav links, the download button/modal flow, and scroll progress bar.
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat critical navigation, layout checks (Garden grid), and the download modal flow on mobile viewport to validate responsive design and tap targets.

notes: Pay special attention to the small_tap_target layout warnings during the mobile phase; measure or visually confirm if the 44px minimum is violated.
Since GitHub and Matrix links point to '#', just verify they do not cause unexpected page jumps or errors when clicked.

prescan_summary.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
prescan_summary.visible_text_excerpt: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V.
